hints: Start by thinking about what you can observe - do members of the same species look similar and live in a way that lets them meet and mate?
Now think about the real test of belonging to one species - what must happen when they breed, and what must be true about the young they produce?
walkthrough:
What Holds a Species Together**
Think of a species as a shared gene pool. Members look similar because they share many genes, and they live in the same place at the same time so they can meet and mate with each other.

The Breeding Test**
The key idea is successful interbreeding. They must be able to mate naturally and produce offspring that are themselves fertile, so genes keep flowing from one generation to the next. That is why population A and population B being genetically distinct and reclassified matters.
Final answer: A group of morphologically similar organisms that interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 - populations A and B are in separate areas of South America. What does that separation stop happening between them?
Compare their habitats - grassland and desert for A, forest for B. How might temperature, camouflage, prey and other factors act differently on coat colour and spots?
Recall where new variation comes from in each isolated group, and why those new variants will not be shared.
Think about who survives and breeds best in each habitat, and what happens to the frequency of helpful alleles over many generations.
Put the long-term result together - what kind of isolation now prevents them interbreeding even if they met again, and what is the name for speciation by geographic separation?
walkthrough:
Separation Stops Gene Flow**
You start with one original population of L. tigrinus. Some barrier separates it into A and B, as shown in Fig. 3.1. With no movement between them there is no interbreeding and no exchange of alleles, so each gene pool evolves independently.

Different Habitats Mean Different Selection**
Population A lives in grassland and desert, population B lives in forest. Light, background for camouflage, climate, prey and predators differ. That is why A has lighter coat colour and different spots from B - each pattern is favoured where it hides the cat best.

Mutation Plus Selection Changes Each Gene Pool**
Random mutations arise separately in A and B. In each place, cats carrying alleles that give better adaptation are more likely to survive, find mates and reproduce, so they pass those advantageous alleles to offspring. Over many generations the frequency of those alleles rises in that population but not in the other.

From Divergence to New Species**
After many generations the two gene pools are genetically distinct. Differences in behaviour, breeding time, genitalia or gametes mean they can no longer produce fertile offspring together. That is reproductive isolation, so B is now L. guttulus. Speciation by geographical separation is called allopatric speciation.

Final answer: Geographical isolation separates populations so no gene flow/interbreeding occurs; different selection pressures/environmental conditions in grassland/desert and forest; different mutations occur in each; individuals with advantageous alleles better adapted, survive and reproduce, passing on alleles; over many generations allele frequencies diverge leading to reproductive isolation; allopatric speciation.

hints: Think about how you get DNA onto a gel to start - where is it loaded and what makes it move at all?
Remember DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphates. Which electrode will it be pulled toward, and what in the gel slows larger pieces more?
Link length to Table 3.1 - Asiatic lion has 22 CA repeats, Bengal tiger 7-8, leopard 14-15. How would comparing how far the sample band travels tell you which species it matches?
walkthrough:
Setting Up Movement**
You load the Ple46 DNA sample into a well at one end of the gel and switch on an electric field. DNA is negatively charged, so it is attracted toward the positive electrode, the anode, at the far end.

Separating by Size**
The gel acts like a sieve. All fragments feel the same pull, but short fragments slip through easily and travel further in the same time, while long fragments are held back. So a Bengal tiger fragment with only 7-8 CA repeats will move furthest, leopard with 14-15 intermediate, and Asiatic lion with 22 repeats shortest distance.

Reading the Result**
After staining, you see bands. By comparing the position, and therefore length, of the unknown sample band with bands from known endangered species or a ladder, you can confirm whether it matches one of the species in Table 3.1.

Final answer: Place DNA sample in well in agarose gel; apply electric field/current; negatively charged DNA moves to anode/positive electrode; shorter fragments with fewer CA repeats move further in a given time; compare position of sample bands with known species to identify source.

hints: Picture a customs officer at a border with bones or skins to check - why would waiting weeks for a distant lab be a problem?
Think about what a small kit linked to a computer database removes - lab equipment, expert time, cost and delay - and how that helps enforcement.
walkthrough:
Built for the Border**
Customs work needs a fast yes-or-no answer while the shipment is held. A small barcoding kit gives a result in minutes to hours at the checkpoint, instead of packaging and sending bones to a distant lab and waiting.

Cheap, Portable and Connected**
The kit is portable and needs no large laboratory, and it is cheaper to run, which helps where funds are limited. Because it links to a computer database that stores many reference sequences, the officer can match the sample quickly and take legal action, which also deters illegal trade.

Final answer: Any two from: quicker test for on-the-spot identification; cheaper, suitable for low income countries; portable, no specialist lab needed, no need to send sample away; many sequences can be stored with bioinformatics for rapid matching.
